full_prose_under_review.title: Conduct Standards for Massachusetts Licensees in 247 CMR 9.01 and 9.03, and the Unified Recovery and Monitoring Program
full_prose_under_review.topic: Professional conduct / General practice standards and advertising under 247 CMR 9.01 and 9.03, and the confidential recovery and monitoring program
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Conformity with pharmacy law in 247 CMR 9.01(1); circumvention in 9.01(2); re-dispensing in 9.01(5); fraudulent or deceptive acts in 9.01(9); aiding or abetting the unlawful practice of pharmacy in 9.01(10); remuneration for referrals or business generation in 9.01(11); dispensing or distributing substandard product to a recipient not licensed or legally authorized to receive it in 9.01(12); the recipient list for a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a hospital or clinic pharmacy without a Drug Store pharmacy license in 9.01(13); blank prescription forms referring to a pharmacist or pharmacy in 9.01(14); carrying, posting or having readily available a license issued by the Board in 9.01(18); the pharmacist's name tag in 9.01(19); the NABP e-profile number in 9.01(20); compliance with a drug's REMS in 9.01(21); false, deceptive or misleading advertising in 9.03; and the Unified Recovery and Monitoring Program under M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G as a confidential, voluntary alternative to discipline for licensees with mental health or substance use concerns, including what became of the Board's former program under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24H
learning_objectives: State whom each paragraph of 247 CMR 9.01 taught here, and 247 CMR 9.03, binds, what each requires or forbids, and any exception each states in its own words.

Apply the affirmative duties in 247 CMR 9.01(1) and (18) through (21): conformity with the laws the paragraph names, the license kept at work, the pharmacist's name tag and NABP e-profile number, and compliance with a drug's REMS.
Apply the intent element and the words either directly or indirectly in 247 CMR 9.01(2).
Recognize a fraudulent or deceptive act under 247 CMR 9.01(9), and distinguish it from advertising that is false, deceptive, or misleading under 247 CMR 9.03.
Apply 247 CMR 9.01(5) to a medication that has been previously dispensed, and 247 CMR 9.01(10) to help given to the unlawful practice of pharmacy.
Take a proposed exchange of value through the actor, counterparty and referral or business-generation elements of 247 CMR 9.01(11), using the 247 CMR 2.00 definition of person.
Distinguish the blank prescription form prohibition in 247 CMR 9.01(14) from the remuneration prohibition in 247 CMR 9.01(11).
Decide under 247 CMR 9.01(12) whether substandard product may go to a given recipient by the recipient's license or legal authorization rather than by purpose or disclosure.
Work a dispensing request at a hospital or clinic pharmacy without a Drug Store pharmacy license through the closed recipient list and the same-household condition in 247 CMR 9.01(13).
Explain the statutory basis of URAMP in M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G, who runs the program, and the two routes by which a licensee enters it.
State what admission to URAMP does and does not do to a pending complaint, to public license status and to practice, keeping the statute separate from the program's published terms.
Identify the limits of URAMP confidentiality and the consequences of withdrawal, termination and successful completion.
Explain what became of the Board's former substance use disorder program under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24H and § 65G(b)(2).

orientation.text: 247 CMR 9.01 is the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's list of general practice standards, and 247 CMR 9.03 adds a one-sentence provision on advertising. This section teaches fourteen of those provisions, and they fall into two groups that are easily blurred. The prohibitions are paragraph (2) on circumvention, paragraph (5) on re-dispensing, paragraph (9) on fraudulent or deceptive acts, paragraph (10) on aiding or abetting the unlawful practice of pharmacy, paragraph (11) on remuneration for referrals or business generation, paragraph (12) on substandard product and its recipients, paragraph (13) on dispensing by a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a hospital or clinic pharmacy without a Drug Store pharmacy license, paragraph (14) on blank prescription forms, and 247 CMR 9.03 on advertising. The affirmative duties are paragraph (1), on conformity with the laws it names, and paragraphs (18) through (21), on the license kept at work, the pharmacist's name tag, the NABP e-profile number and compliance with a drug's REMS. Each provision has its own addressee, its own act and, only where its words state one, its own exception, and none of them borrows a condition from another.

Most of the fourteen provisions are addressed to a licensee. 247 CMR 2.00, whose definitions apply throughout 247 CMR, does not define that word. Read in its ordinary sense it reaches whoever holds a license or registration issued by the Board, a pharmacy as much as an individual, and because no definition settles the point the safe course is to treat every such holder as bound. The rest name their addressee: paragraph (13) a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, the hospital or clinic pharmacy; paragraphs (19), (20) and (21) a pharmacist; and paragraph (18) a pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and pharmacy technician. The neighbouring paragraphs of 247 CMR 9.01 are taught elsewhere: current United States Pharmacopeia standards, practice within the scope of education, training and experience, the limit on refusing to compound and confidentiality in paragraphs (3), (4), (15) and (16) with the general practice standards; returned medications and drug samples in paragraphs (6) and (7) with returns, recalls and product integrity; and the practice-hour ceiling in paragraph (17) with the pharmacy internship. Paragraph (8), under which a pharmacist while on duty shall be responsible for the proper preservation, storage, and security of all controlled substances in the pharmacy, concerns the security of controlled stock, the subject of Securing Controlled Stock, Reporting Theft or Loss, and Disposing of It Lawfully.

Two provisions point outward to the rest of pharmacy law. Paragraph (1) provides that a licensee shall conduct professional activities in conformity with M.G.L. c. 112, §§ 24 through 42D, M.G.L. c. 94C, and 247 CMR 2.00: Definitions. It is an affirmative duty whose content lies in the bodies of law it names rather than in the paragraph itself. Paragraph (10) provides that a licensee may not in any way aid or abet the unlawful practice of pharmacy. The paragraph does not define the unlawful practice of pharmacy, so whether the conduct being helped is unlawful practice is decided by the licensure and scope rules that govern the person being helped, and the words in any way reach aiding or abetting by whatever means it is done. The separate ground for Board discipline that reaches knowingly permitting, aiding or abetting unlicensed activity is taught in Grounds for Board Discipline and the Credentials It Reaches, together with the other grounds on which the Board may act.

Paragraph (2) provides that a licensee may not process a prescription; dispense a drug, device, or other substance; or administer a controlled substance or vaccine in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy. Three features of that sentence decide cases. Its object is any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy, so it is not confined to the Board's own regulations. Its element is intention: it attaches to the manner in which one of the three named acts is carried out and to what that manner is intended to achieve, so an inadvertent departure from a rule is not what it describes, although that departure may break the underlying rule itself. And it expressly includes circumvention intended indirectly, so a manner of processing, dispensing or administering that is intended to reach by a roundabout route what a law or regulation forbids is within its words, however lawful each separate step looks when taken alone. Whether a prescription is valid in the first place, and the pharmacist's corresponding responsibility for it, are taught with prescription validity.

Paragraph (9) is the shortest in the group: a licensee may not engage in any fraudulent or deceptive act. It defines neither word and states no further condition. Nothing in it confines the prohibition to prescriptions, records, billing or any other setting, and nothing in it asks whether anyone was in fact misled, relied on the act or lost anything by it, whether the licensee gained, or whether some other rule was broken at the same time. An arrangement built to leave a false impression can be a deceptive act in the ordinary sense of the word even where each entry in it, read alone, is literally accurate. Paragraph (9) and paragraph (2) are separate prohibitions and the same facts can engage both: paragraph (2) is framed around a manner intended to circumvent a law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy, paragraph (9) around a fraudulent or deceptive act, and neither makes a breach of the other a condition. Which product may be dispensed in place of the one prescribed, and what the purchaser is charged, are governed by the product-selection rules taught separately.

247 CMR 9.03 addresses one setting in a single sentence: a licensee may not engage in any advertising that is false, deceptive, or misleading. The three descriptions are joined by or, so an advertisement need not be false to be caught; one that is deceptive, or one that is misleading, is within the section as well. The section defines none of the three words and states no exception. It sits beside paragraph (9) rather than inside it: paragraph (9) reaches any fraudulent or deceptive act, 247 CMR 9.03 reaches advertising that is false, deceptive, or misleading, and a deceptive advertisement can engage both.

Paragraph (5) provides that, unless otherwise permitted by law, regulation, or Board policy, a licensee may not re-dispense any medication which has been previously dispensed. Its words turn on the medication's having been previously dispensed and say nothing about the medication's condition, its packaging or whether its container was opened. The prohibition yields to three sources of permission, law, regulation or Board policy, and the paragraph does not itself say which of them permits re-dispensing or when. Dispensing, as 247 CMR 2.00 defines it, is the physical act of delivering a drug, chemical, device or combination thereof to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, so a medication that has been through that act has been previously dispensed. Whether a pharmacy must or may accept a medication that a patient brings back, and what then happens to it, are taught with returns, recalls and product integrity.

Paragraph (11) is built from four parts, and each of them limits it. The actor is a licensee and the verbs are offer, solicit, or receive, so the paragraph runs in both directions: the licensee may be the one offering value or the one soliciting or receiving it. What passes is remuneration or anything of value, so goods, services and hospitality are as much within it as money. The other party is any person who owns, operates, manages, or is an employee of a hospital, nursing home, or other health care facility, and under 247 CMR 2.00 a person is an individual, corporation, government, governmental subdivision or agency, business trust, estate trust, partnership or association, or any other legal entity. The exchange must be in return for one of two things: a referral to a pharmacy, pharmacist, pharmacy technician, or pharmacy intern, or the generation of business from sale or furnishing of any drugs, devices, or services to any such persons or institutions. The second limb needs no individual patient to be referred, so value offered to a facility's manager in return for the facility's drug business is inside it. The paragraph states no exception: it names no threshold of value, no cure by disclosure and no allowance for an arrangement described as marketing. It does not define other health care facility, and it says nothing about an exchange with someone who has no such connection. It is a Board regulation that stands on its own words and refers to no other law.

Paragraph (14) provides that a licensee may not provide any practitioner with blank prescription forms which refer to any pharmacist or pharmacy. Under 247 CMR 2.00 a practitioner is any person with prescriptive privileges as defined in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 1. What makes the forms forbidden is that they are blank prescription forms and that they refer to a pharmacist or pharmacy, and the act forbidden is providing them. Unlike paragraph (11), paragraph (14) has no element of value or of anything given in return: it does not ask whether the forms were paid for or free, whether there was any agreement with the practitioner, or whether any patient was in fact steered, and it states no exception. Because it speaks of any pharmacist or pharmacy, the forms need not name the licensee's own pharmacy. The paragraph says nothing about forms that a practitioner signs in advance; what a prescription must carry to be valid is taught with prescription validity.

Paragraph (12) provides that a licensee may not dispense or distribute any expired, outdated, defective, contaminated, counterfeit, contraband, or otherwise substandard drug or device to any person or entity who is not licensed or legally authorized to receive such drug or device. The list of conditions ends in otherwise substandard, so it is not closed. The test is the recipient's status, not the purpose of the transfer: a worthy destination such as a charity or a training exercise does not help if the recipient is neither licensed nor legally authorized to receive the product, and the paragraph offers no cure by telling the recipient that the product is expired. Nor does the paragraph forbid every transfer of such product, because a recipient licensed or legally authorized to receive it is outside the prohibition; the paragraph does not itself say who that is, and other law decides it. What the recipient must be licensed or legally authorized to do is receive such drug or device, so neither employment by the pharmacy nor a license to do something else supplies the authorization. Dispensing, as 247 CMR 2.00 defines it, is the physical act of delivering a drug, chemical or device to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, and paragraph (12) names dispensing among the acts it forbids. Nothing in the paragraph treats a prescription as authority to receive a substandard unit of the drug, and the course that is safe on any reading is that such product is not dispensed to a patient.

Paragraph (13) applies in a defined setting and to a defined person. Unless otherwise permitted by law, a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a hospital or clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy license may not dispense drugs to any person other than inpatients or outpatients of the hospital or clinic, or to employees of said hospital or clinic, or to said employees' spouses and children who live in the same household with said employees. The list is closed and it is built on relationship to the institution. Inpatients and outpatients of the hospital or clinic are on it, and so are its employees. The family limb names two relationships, spouse and children, and attaches the same condition to both: they must live in the same household with the employee. An employee's parent or sibling is not on the list even when living in that household, and an employee's spouse or child who lives elsewhere is not on it either. The paragraph speaks of recipients, not prescribers, so a prescription written by one of the institution's own practitioners adds no one to the list, and it says nothing about price or payment. Its opening words make the limit yield where other law permits dispensing to someone else, and a hospital or clinic pharmacy that holds a Drug Store pharmacy license is outside the paragraph's terms.

Three paragraphs deal with how licensed people are identified at work. Paragraph (18) provides that a pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and pharmacy technician shall carry, post on the wall of the pharmacy where he or she works, or have readily available at the pharmacy where he or she works, a license issued by the Board. It binds all three roles, and it gives three ways of meeting the duty joined by or, so posting the license on the wall is one option rather than the requirement. Paragraph (19) provides that a pharmacist shall wear a name tag with at least his or her first name and the title "Pharmacist", "Registered Pharmacist", or "R.Ph.". The words at least set a minimum: the first name and one of the three listed titles must appear, the paragraph does not require a last name, and a tag that shows a degree or another title in place of one of the three listed titles does not meet its words. Paragraph (20) provides that a pharmacist shall maintain an NABP e-profile number, NABP being, under 247 CMR 2.00, the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy. 247 CMR 2.00 separately defines a differently worded term, NABP Number, as a unique seven digit number issued by the National Council for Prescription Drug Programs, and paragraph (20) does not use that term. Paragraphs (19) and (20) bind the pharmacist; name tags for pharmacy support personnel are taught in Massachusetts Pharmacy Support Personnel: Supervisory Ratios, Identification and Schedule II Handling.

Paragraph (21) provides that a pharmacist shall comply with all elements of a drug's FDA required risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS), including any distribution or dispensing restriction included in its REMS. The REMS itself is federal and particular to the drug, but the duty to comply with it is also a Massachusetts practice standard: the paragraph takes in all of the REMS's elements and names distribution and dispensing restrictions expressly, so a pharmacist who dispenses in breach of such a restriction falls short of the Board's standard as well as of the REMS. What a REMS may require, and the pharmacy's part in particular REMS programs, are federal subjects taught in Medication Guides and REMS at the Pharmacy Counter: 21 CFR Part 208, the Mifepristone REMS and the Removed Clozapine REMS.

The Unified Recovery and Monitoring Program, known as URAMP, is described on its program pages as a confidential, voluntary recovery and monitoring program for health professionals licensed through the boards overseen by the Bureau of Health Professions Licensure, and it rests on statute. M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(b)(1), inserted by St. 2022, c. 177, § 36, requires the department of public health to establish a voluntary program for monitoring the rehabilitation of licensed health care professionals who seek support for their mental health or substance use or who are referred to the program by a licensing board. The program is the department's rather than the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's: the department employs its program director, and a rehabilitation evaluation committee appointed by the commissioner evaluates requests to participate and makes recommendations. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(a) a licensed health care professional is an individual who holds a license, a license includes a registration, authorization or certificate issued by a board of registration, and a licensing board is the board that issued it. M.G.L. c. 13, § 9(a) places the board of registration in pharmacy among the boards serving in the department, so an individual holding a license or registration from that Board is within the statute's description, while a pharmacy, not being an individual, is not. There are two ways in: the professional may come forward seeking support, or a licensing board may refer the professional. The program's Frequently Asked Questions page states that URAMP is established in accordance with Chapter 177 of the Acts of 2022, An Act Addressing Barriers to Care for Mental Health.

Entry has conditions, and admission does not by itself end a pending matter. Under § 65G(f) a professional who applies, or who is referred by the licensing board, shall specify, in a form and format set by the department, the mental health condition or substance use that the professional believes may impede or has affected the ability to safely practice, and shall agree to comply, to the best of the professional's ability, with an individualized rehabilitation plan to be admitted. The committee evaluates a request within 5 business days of receiving it and recommends on admission, and the director admits eligible professionals and gives each participant a written plan with requirements for supervision and surveillance. Under § 65G(g) the licensing board may dismiss any pending investigation or complaint against the participant that arises from or relates to the participant's mental health or substance use, and may change the participant's publicly-available license status to reflect the existence of non-disciplinary restrictions or conditions. Under the proviso that closes § 65G(e), any restriction or condition relating to a participant's professional practice required under that subsection, and any change to one, is subject to the approval of the participant's licensing board. The word may leaves dismissal to the board, and a complaint that neither arises from nor relates to the mental health or substance use is outside that power. The program's guidance manual, as read on 16 September 2026, describes URAMP as able to function as an alternative to disciplinary proceedings where evidence indicates that the incident happened as a result of, or in connection with, a substance use disorder or mental health condition, and describes the practice: upon effective enrollment, pending complaints based on facts related to the incidents that led to enrollment are dismissed by the licensing board without prejudice; while an application is pending the complaint resolution process continues; and where admission is not granted the case is remitted to the Bureau of Health Professions Licensure investigators to determine whether disciplinary proceedings are required. The manual also describes a referral by licensing board investigators as not necessarily meaning entry, and as unlikely to be appropriate where a professional has diverted drugs for sale or distribution to others, caused harm to a patient because of their abuse, or engaged in behavior with a high potential for causing harm, such as substituting or tampering with patients' drugs.

Participation does not leave practice untouched, but it need not keep a participant out of practice for the whole agreement, and both the program's terms and the statute say what follows if participation fails. Under the manual, once the application is received the licensing board changes the license status online to non-disciplinary restriction, meaning the applicant is not permitted to practice; the status is published in the licensee database without the reasons and remains upon effective enrollment, and where admission is being considered as an alternative to discipline the applicant is asked to sign a legally binding agreement not to practice during that period. That status is not the whole story, because both the statute and the manual provide for practice during participation. Under § 65G(d)(2)(iv) the rehabilitation evaluation committee makes recommendations for each participant as to whether the participant may continue or resume professional practice within the full scope of the license, and under the proviso to § 65G(e) any restriction or condition on the participant's practice, and any change to one, needs the licensing board's approval. The manual, as read on 17 September 2026 (its PDF is dated 29 January 2026), describes the usual course: all admissions carry an out of practice consideration; a participant entering for a complaint based on a substance use disorder normally requires a restriction from practice for the first six months, with gradual return to work privileges granted as the participant continues to meet the program's compliance criteria, while for a complaint based on mental health functioning the admission evaluator and/or the rehabilitation evaluation committee determines how long the restriction lasts. Practice privileges are restored by the program before practice resumes; a return to practice requires a supervisor agreement and quarterly supervisor employment reports; a change to the consent agreement, such as a return to practice, is reviewed and approved by URAMP staff or the committee; the licensing board authorizes the director to change the license status in accordance with the consent agreement; and a return to practice approved by staff or the committee during or at the end of the program is put before the licensing board for final approval. Applicants must admit to having problems with substance use and/or accept that mental health is currently impacting their practice, and agree to waive all rights to appeal, file grievances or complaints, and contest licensure actions relating to or arising from their participation. The URAMP Consent Agreement for Participants is a legally binding document, effective when countersigned by URAMP staff, that runs five years with an opportunity for early discharge at the three-year mark and in which the participant agrees to surrender the license voluntarily if participation ends by withdrawal or by termination for noncompliance; the manual adds that a participant may withdraw at any point and that the licensing board will then proceed with disciplinary action in relation to the underlying complaint. The statute supplies the director's power to terminate a participant for noncompliance with the plan or for material misrepresentations, with the condition that noncompliance may result in termination only if the plan states that it will, and it lets the licensing board immediately suspend the license as is necessary to protect the public health, safety and welfare on notice from the director that the participant has withdrawn before completion or has been terminated.

URAMP is confidential, but the confidentiality has stated limits. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(a) and (h) the record of participation, meaning the materials received and reviewed by the director, the rehabilitation evaluation committee or a licensing board in connection with an application and with a participant's progress and compliance, is not a public record, is exempt from disclosure under clause Twenty-sixth of M.G.L. c. 4, § 7 and M.G.L. c. 66, and is to be kept confidential and not subject to subpoena or discovery in any civil, criminal, legislative or administrative proceeding without the prior written consent of the participant or applicant. The statute states where that stops. If a professional referred by a licensing board fails to complete the application process, a licensing board may use information and documents in the record as evidence in a disciplinary proceeding as necessary to protect public health, safety and welfare. And under § 65G(e)(viii), where the professional was referred by a licensing board, or is the subject of a pending or completed investigation or complaint arising from or relating to mental health or substance use, the director reports the name and license number to the licensing board on a failure to complete the admission process, on admission, on termination, on withdrawal before completion, and on the initial practice restrictions or conditions in the plan and any change to or removal of them, with the basis. The manual adds program-level limits and assurances: the licensing board may obtain pertinent records of participation at any point during participation; information from an applicant who decides not to participate after applying may be used by the board in connection with a subsequent disciplinary action where it is relevant to the matter under investigation; records of participation, including the application, are not subject to public records requests; participants admitted into URAMP are not reported in public or to any disciplinary database; and participant matters before the committee and the licensing board are heard in executive session.

Successful completion has its own consequences. Under § 65G(h), once the rehabilitation evaluation committee determines that a participant has successfully completed the program and that the participant's ability to safely practice is not impaired or affected by mental health or substance use, the department, the program, the committee and the licensing board, if applicable, seal all records pertaining to the participation, and the records of participation of participants who successfully complete the program are destroyed 3 years following the date of successful completion. The manual describes the same stage from the participant's side: when the licensing board has approved successful discharge all URAMP records are sealed and any related complaints are dismissed, and upon successful completion program conditions end and the license status changes to current.

URAMP also answers what became of the Board's own program. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24H(a) provides that the board of registration in pharmacy shall establish a rehabilitation program for registered pharmacists, pharmacy interns and pharmacy technicians who have a substance use issue, and § 24H(b)(i) provides that the program shall serve as a voluntary alternative to traditional disciplinary actions. M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(b)(2) then provides that a board of registration required by another requirement of chapter 112 to establish a similar rehabilitation program shall fulfill that requirement by formally adopting the department's program in lieu of establishing its own. The program's pages describe the result: the Board's Pharmacy Substance Use Disorder Program, PSUD, and the nursing board's Substance Addiction Recovery Program transitioned to URAMP when it launched in December 2024, the URAMP Frequently Asked Questions page giving December 16, 2024 as the date, and URAMP absorbed both, with all monitoring program participation managed by the URAMP team. The same page describes PSUD as a confidential, voluntary program for licensed professionals with substance use disorders that impact their practice, and URAMP as also available to licensees with mental health concerns not related to substance use disorders that have the potential to impact their practice. Impairment as a ground for discipline, and the process by which a complaint is investigated and decided, are taught in the treatment of Board discipline.

Licensed health care professionals who seek support for their mental health or substance use, or who are referred by a licensing board; a license includes a registration issued by the board of registration in pharmacy

Available to licensees who seek support or are referred by their licensing board; applicants must admit to having problems with substance use and/or accept that mental health is currently impacting their practice
Condition of admission

Specify the mental health condition or substance use believed to impede or to have affected safe practice, and agree to comply, to the best of one's ability, with an individualized rehabilitation plan

Sign the URAMP Consent Agreement for Participants, including agreement to surrender the license voluntarily on withdrawal or on termination for noncompliance, and waive all rights to appeal, file grievances or complaints, and contest licensure actions arising from participation
Pending complaint
The licensing board may dismiss a pending investigation or complaint that arises from or relates to the mental health or substance use

On effective enrollment, pending complaints based on facts related to the incidents that led to enrollment are dismissed without prejudice; the complaint resolution process continues while an application is pending
Public license status and practice

The licensing board may change the publicly-available status to reflect non-disciplinary restrictions or conditions; the rehabilitation evaluation committee recommends whether a participant may continue or resume practice within the full scope of the license; and restrictions or conditions on practice, and changes to them, need the licensing board's approval

Status becomes non-disciplinary restriction on receipt of the application, meaning the applicant is not permitted to practice, and is published without the reasons; during participation practice privileges are restored by the program before practice resumes, normally after six months of compliance under a substance use disorder agreement and for a mental health complaint after a period set by the admission evaluator and/or the committee, with a supervisor agreement and final approval by the licensing board
Withdrawal or termination

The director may terminate for noncompliance with the plan or for material misrepresentations, but noncompliance may result in termination only if the plan states that it will; on notice of withdrawal or termination the licensing board may immediately suspend the license as necessary to protect the public
A participant may withdraw at any point, and the licensing board will then proceed with disciplinary action in relation to the underlying complaint
Confidentiality and its limits

The record of participation is not a public record and is not subject to subpoena or discovery without prior written consent; a licensing board may use it as evidence where a professional it referred fails to complete the application; the director reports name and license number in board-referred or complaint-related cases

Records not subject to public records requests; participants not reported in public or to any disciplinary database; executive session; the licensing board may obtain pertinent records during participation
Successful completion

Records sealed on the committee's determination of successful completion and unimpaired ability to practice safely; records of participation destroyed 3 years following the date of successful completion
On board-approved discharge all URAMP records are sealed and related complaints dismissed; program conditions end and the license status changes to current

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist employed by a clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy license receives four requests in one afternoon: a prescription for a clinic outpatient; one for the husband of a clinic receptionist, who lives with her; one for the receptionist's mother, who also lives with her; and one for the adult son of a clinic nurse, who has his own apartment across town and whose prescription was written by a clinic physician. The pharmacist proposes to fill all four because each patient has some connection to the clinic. Which may be dispensed?
steps: Identify the addressee and the setting. 247 CMR 9.01(13) is addressed to a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a hospital or clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy license, so it governs this pharmacist.

Read the list as closed. Unless otherwise permitted by law, the pharmacist may not dispense drugs to any person other than inpatients or outpatients of the clinic, employees of the clinic, or those employees' spouses and children who live in the same household with the employees.
The outpatient is on the list, and the receptionist's husband is the spouse of an employee living in the same household with her, so both prescriptions may be dispensed.
The receptionist's mother lives in the same household, but the family limb names spouses and children only, so sharing the household does not bring a parent onto the list.

The nurse's son is the child of an employee, but he does not live in the same household with her. That a clinic physician wrote his prescription does not help, because the paragraph lists recipients and says nothing about prescribers.
Nothing in the facts shows other law permitting dispensing to the mother or the son, so the opening words of the paragraph do not change the result.
worked_examples.resolution: The outpatient's and the husband's prescriptions may be dispensed; the mother's and the son's may not. The error the scenario invites is reading the family limb as covering any relative in the household or any child of an employee wherever he lives, or treating a clinic prescriber as enlarging a list that is defined by the recipient.

worked_examples.scenario: A community pharmacy's manager proposes three initiatives: a gift card for each discharge planner employed by a nearby hospital for every patient the planner sends to the pharmacy; a catered lunch for the director of nursing of a nursing home whose medication supply contract the pharmacy wants to win; and free pads of blank prescription forms printed with the pharmacy's name and telephone number for the physicians of a local practice, with nothing asked in return. The manager argues that no cash changes hands, that the lunch involves no patient referral, and that the pads are simply a free convenience. How does 247 CMR 9.01 treat each proposal?
steps: Start with paragraph (11): a licensee may not offer, solicit, or receive remuneration or anything of value to or from any person who owns, operates, manages, or is an employee of a hospital, nursing home, or other health care facility in return for a referral to a pharmacy, pharmacist, pharmacy technician, or pharmacy intern or the generation of business from sale or furnishing of any drugs, devices, or services to any such persons or institutions.

The gift cards are anything of value, the discharge planners are employees of a hospital, and the cards are offered in return for referrals to the pharmacy, so every element of the referral limb is present and the absence of cash is irrelevant.

The lunch is also anything of value, the director of nursing is an employee of a nursing home, and the lunch is offered in return for the generation of business from furnishing drugs to that institution, which is the second limb; no individual patient referral is needed.

The pads fall under paragraph (14), not paragraph (11): a licensee may not provide any practitioner with blank prescription forms which refer to any pharmacist or pharmacy, and the physicians, as persons with prescriptive privileges, are practitioners under 247 CMR 2.00.

Paragraph (14) has no element of value or of anything given in return, so it does not matter that the pads are free and that nothing is asked; the forms are blank and refer to a pharmacy, and providing them is the forbidden act.
The pharmacy is a licensee on the ordinary reading of that word, and each proposal would be its own act, so none of the three may proceed.
worked_examples.resolution: All three are prohibited: the gift cards under the referral limb of 247 CMR 9.01(11), the lunch under its business-generation limb, and the pads under 247 CMR 9.01(14). The error the scenario invites is reading a cash or individual-referral requirement into paragraph (11), or carrying paragraph (11)'s requirement of something given in return over to paragraph (14), which has none.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy is clearing a shelf of expired inhalers and a box of blood glucose meters that failed the manufacturer's accuracy check. A pharmacy technician asks to take two expired inhalers home to show her family how a spacer works; an unlicensed volunteer group collecting supplies for a disaster area offers to take the rest if the pharmacy marks them as expired; and a regular patient with a current prescription asks to buy one of the expired inhalers at a discount. Which of the three requests may go ahead under 247 CMR 9.01(12)?
steps: Classify the product. Expired inhalers are expired drugs, and meters that failed the accuracy check are defective or otherwise substandard devices, so the paragraph is engaged.

Apply the recipient test. A licensee may not dispense or distribute such product to any person or entity who is not licensed or legally authorized to receive such drug or device, so the question for each request is the recipient's status, not the reason for the request.
The technician's license to work as a technician is not a license or legal authorization to receive expired product, and neither is her employment, so the training purpose does not help.

The volunteer group is not licensed, and nothing in the facts shows any other legal authorization to receive the product; marking the product as expired changes nothing, because the paragraph has no cure by disclosure.

For the patient, dispensing under 247 CMR 2.00 is delivery to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, and paragraph (12) names dispensing among the acts it forbids. Nothing in the paragraph treats a prescription as authority to receive substandard product, so the course that is safe on any reading is not to dispense the expired inhaler, whatever the price.

The paragraph does not forbid every movement of such product: a recipient licensed or legally authorized to receive it is outside the prohibition, so the pharmacy's route for this stock is to such a recipient, identified under the law that authorizes it.
worked_examples.resolution: None of the three requests may go ahead. The error the scenario invites is sorting the requests by the worthiness of the purpose or by disclosure, instead of asking whether each recipient is licensed or legally authorized to receive the substandard product.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist at a hospital pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy license is asked by a hospital employee to fill a prescription written for the employee's brother, who does not live with him and is not a hospital patient. To make the dispensing look like dispensing to an eligible recipient, the pharmacist enters the brother's prescription in the pharmacy system under the employee's name and hands the medication to the employee to pass on. Every field in the record is completed, and the employee is himself on the permitted list. What has the pharmacist done?
steps: Start with the underlying limit. Under 247 CMR 9.01(13), unless otherwise permitted by law, the pharmacist may not dispense drugs to anyone other than the hospital's inpatients or outpatients, its employees, or employees' spouses and children who live in the same household with them. A brother is not on that list, and nothing in the facts shows other law permitting dispensing to him.

Look past the record. Dispensing under 247 CMR 2.00 is delivery to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner; the prescription was written for the brother and the medication is meant for him, so entering it under the employee's name changes the record, not the recipient.

Apply 247 CMR 9.01(2). The pharmacist dispensed a drug in a manner intended, indirectly, to circumvent a regulation governing the practice of pharmacy, and the lawful appearance of handing a medication to an eligible employee does not answer a paragraph that looks to what the manner was intended to achieve.

Apply 247 CMR 9.01(9). Entering the prescription under the employee's name is designed to make the record show a dispensing that did not happen, which is a deceptive act; the paragraph does not ask whether anyone reviewing the record was in fact misled.
The three paragraphs are separate prohibitions, and one set of facts can engage all of them.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist has dispensed outside the list in 247 CMR 9.01(13), in a manner intended to circumvent that paragraph contrary to 247 CMR 9.01(2), and by a deceptive act contrary to 247 CMR 9.01(9). The error the scenario invites is treating the record, which names an eligible employee, as showing that the dispensing complied.

worked_examples.scenario: Before a new community pharmacy opens, its manager proposes five arrangements: staff pharmacists will wear name tags showing only a surname and a degree, such as 'Dr. Lee, PharmD'; the pharmacists' Board licenses will be posted on the wall of the pharmacy, while each pharmacy technician will keep his or her license at home; a window banner will read 'Lowest prices in Massachusetts', although the manager knows that two nearby pharmacies charge less for most prescriptions; a newly hired pharmacist who has no NABP e-profile number will obtain one only if the Board asks; and a drug whose REMS restricts dispensing to pharmacies certified in that REMS will be dispensed from the first day, although the pharmacy has not been certified. Which of the arrangements meet 247 CMR 9.01 and 9.03?
steps: Name tags. 247 CMR 9.01(19) provides that a pharmacist shall wear a name tag with at least his or her first name and the title "Pharmacist", "Registered Pharmacist", or "R.Ph.". A tag showing a surname and a degree has neither the first name nor one of the three titles, so it does not meet the paragraph.

Licenses. 247 CMR 9.01(18) provides that a pharmacist, pharmacy intern, and pharmacy technician shall carry, post on the wall of the pharmacy where he or she works, or have readily available at the pharmacy where he or she works, a license issued by the Board. Posting the pharmacists' licenses meets it for them; a technician whose license is at home neither carries it, nor has it posted, nor has it readily available at the pharmacy.

Advertising. Under 247 CMR 9.03 a licensee may not engage in any advertising that is false, deceptive, or misleading. A claim to the lowest prices that the manager knows to be untrue is false, and the pharmacy, a licensee on the ordinary reading of that word, may not run it.

NABP e-profile. 247 CMR 9.01(20) provides that a pharmacist shall maintain an NABP e-profile number, and the paragraph attaches no condition of a request from the Board, so a pharmacist without one is not meeting it.

REMS. 247 CMR 9.01(21) provides that a pharmacist shall comply with all elements of a drug's FDA required REMS, including any distribution or dispensing restriction included in its REMS. Dispensing in breach of a REMS restriction to certified pharmacies falls short of that duty; the federal side of the REMS is taught with Medication Guides and REMS.
worked_examples.resolution: Only the posting of the pharmacists' licenses meets the provisions. The error the scenario invites is treating these provisions as formalities: a degree does not replace the first name and one of the three listed titles, a license left at home is not carried, posted or readily available at the pharmacy, a price claim known to be untrue is false advertising, the e-profile duty does not wait for the Board to ask, and a REMS dispensing restriction is also a Massachusetts duty under 247 CMR 9.01(21).

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist is the subject of a pending complaint to the Board after she was found unsteady at work and later disclosed an alcohol use problem. A colleague tells her four things about URAMP: that she cannot apply unless the Board refers her; that admission will wipe out every complaint on her record; that nothing about it will appear in the public license lookup; and that if the program does not suit her she can leave with no consequence. How accurate is that advice?
steps: Check who may seek entry. M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(b)(1) covers licensed health care professionals who seek support for their mental health or substance use as well as those referred by a licensing board, and under § 65G(a) a license includes a license or registration issued by a board of registration; M.G.L. c. 13, § 9(a) places the board of registration in pharmacy among those boards. She may come forward herself.

Admission has conditions. She must specify, in the department's form and format, the substance use she believes may impede or has affected her ability to practice safely, and agree to comply, to the best of her ability, with an individualized rehabilitation plan; under the program's terms she also signs the URAMP Consent Agreement for Participants.

Admission does not wipe out every complaint. Under § 65G(g) the licensing board may dismiss a pending investigation or complaint that arises from or relates to her mental health or substance use, and the program's manual describes pending complaints based on the facts that led to enrollment as dismissed without prejudice on effective enrollment; a complaint unconnected with her substance use is outside that power.

Something will appear publicly. The statute lets the licensing board change her publicly-available license status to reflect non-disciplinary restrictions or conditions, and under the program's terms the status becomes non-disciplinary restriction on receipt of her application, meaning she may not practice, and is published without the reasons; that is not a bar for the whole program, since the manual describes a restriction from practice normally for the first six months under a substance use disorder agreement, with privileges then restored by the program and final approval by the licensing board.

Leaving after admission has consequences. On notice from the director that she has withdrawn before completion, the licensing board may immediately suspend her license as necessary to protect the public health, safety and welfare; the manual states that the board will then proceed with disciplinary action on the underlying complaint; and the consent agreement records her agreement to surrender her license voluntarily if she withdraws.
worked_examples.resolution: All four statements are wrong. The error the scenario invites is treating URAMP either as a program a licensee can reach only through the Board or as an amnesty that clears the record, stays invisible and can be abandoned without cost; it is a voluntary, confidential program whose effect on a pending complaint reaches related matters and rests with the licensing board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(1), with what must a licensee's professional activities conform?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 112, §§ 24 through 42D, M.G.L. c. 94C, and 247 CMR 2.00: Definitions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which of the provisions taught here is addressed to a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a particular kind of pharmacy, and what kind?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.01(13), addressed to a pharmacist connected with, or employed by, a hospital or clinic pharmacy that does not hold a Drug Store pharmacy license.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(2), which three acts are prohibited when carried out in a manner intended to circumvent a law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Processing a prescription; dispensing a drug, device, or other substance; and administering a controlled substance or vaccine.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: 247 CMR 9.01(2) reaches only circumvention of the Board's own regulations, and only direct circumvention.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False on both counts. Its object is any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy, and it covers a manner intended either directly or indirectly to circumvent.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(5), when may a licensee re-dispense a medication that has been previously dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only where law, regulation, or Board policy otherwise permits it; otherwise the paragraph forbids re-dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Beyond the act itself, what further condition does 247 CMR 9.01(9) state before a fraudulent or deceptive act is prohibited?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None. A licensee may not engage in any fraudulent or deceptive act, and the paragraph names no requirement of reliance, loss, gain, a particular setting or a separate violation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.03, must an advertisement be false before a licensee is barred from engaging in it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A licensee may not engage in any advertising that is false, deceptive, or misleading.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.01(10) forbid, and does the paragraph define the unlawful practice of pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Aiding or abetting, in any way, the unlawful practice of pharmacy; no, the paragraph does not define it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three verbs and the two purposes in 247 CMR 9.01(11).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Offer, solicit, or receive; in return for a referral to a pharmacy, pharmacist, pharmacy technician, or pharmacy intern, or for the generation of business from sale or furnishing of any drugs, devices, or services to the facility-connected persons or institutions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who must be on the other side of an exchange for 247 CMR 9.01(11) to apply, and can that be a company?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any person who owns, operates, manages, or is an employee of a hospital, nursing home, or other health care facility; yes, because under 247 CMR 2.00 a person includes a corporation or any other legal entity as well as an individual.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: 247 CMR 9.01(11) requires a cash payment.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. It reaches remuneration or anything of value.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A licensee gives a prescriber free blank prescription forms printed with a pharmacy's name and asks for nothing. Which paragraph applies, and does the absence of payment matter?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.01(14); no. A licensee may not provide any practitioner with blank prescription forms which refer to any pharmacist or pharmacy, and the paragraph has no element of payment, agreement or steering.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does 247 CMR 9.01(14) address prescription forms that a practitioner signs in advance?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Its subject is blank prescription forms which refer to any pharmacist or pharmacy, provided to any practitioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(12), what decides whether expired stock may be distributed to a particular recipient?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whether the recipient is licensed or legally authorized to receive such drug or device; the purpose of the transfer and any disclosure to the recipient do not decide it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: 247 CMR 9.01(12) forbids every transfer of expired product out of a pharmacy.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. It forbids dispensing or distributing such product to a person or entity not licensed or legally authorized to receive it; a licensed or legally authorized recipient is outside the prohibition.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: At a hospital pharmacy without a Drug Store pharmacy license, may the pharmacist dispense to an employee's spouse who lives at a separate address?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No, unless other law permits it. The family limb of 247 CMR 9.01(13) covers employees' spouses and children who live in the same household with the employees.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three ways 247 CMR 9.01(18) allows a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician to meet the license duty.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Carry the license issued by the Board, post it on the wall of the pharmacy where he or she works, or have it readily available at that pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist's name tag reading 'J. Smith, PharmD' meets 247 CMR 9.01(19).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The name tag must show at least the first name and the title "Pharmacist", "Registered Pharmacist", or "R.Ph.".

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.01(20) require a pharmacist to maintain, and what is NABP under 247 CMR 2.00?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An NABP e-profile number; NABP means the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is compliance with a drug's REMS only a federal matter for a pharmacist in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 247 CMR 9.01(21) requires a pharmacist to comply with all elements of a drug's FDA required REMS, including any distribution or dispensing restriction included in its REMS.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which statute underlies URAMP, and who must establish the program it requires?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G, inserted by St. 2022, c. 177, § 36, requires the department of public health to establish the voluntary program; the program's FAQ states that URAMP is established in accordance with Chapter 177 of the Acts of 2022.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the two routes into URAMP?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A licensed health care professional may seek support for mental health or substance use, or may be referred to the program by a licensing board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: upon admission to URAMP the licensing board must dismiss every pending complaint against the participant.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(g) the licensing board may dismiss a pending investigation or complaint that arises from or relates to the participant's mental health or substance use; the program's manual describes such complaints as dismissed without prejudice on effective enrollment.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When does M.G.L. c. 112, § 65G(h) allow a licensing board to use information in the record of participation as evidence in a disciplinary proceeding?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When a licensed health care professional referred to the program by a licensing board fails to complete the application process, as necessary to protect public health, safety and welfare.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What may the licensing board do on notice from the director that a participant has withdrawn before completion or been terminated?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Immediately suspend the participant's license as is necessary to protect the public health, safety and welfare.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What license status does the URAMP manual describe on receipt of an application, and what does it mean?
